did_you_know.text: Amos’s first vision takes place at the beginning of the late-rain season. He sees a swarm of locusts forming after the king’s mowings have already been harvested. The vision portrays a threat to the vegetation and the food supply.
Amos prays, “Please forgive, Lord. How can Jacob survive? He is so small.” The name “Jacob” here refers to the people of Israel, emphasizing their weakness and vulnerability in the face of disaster.

After Amos’s prayer, it is said that the Lord relented concerning the disaster, and it would not happen. Thus, the vision highlights the power of prayer and the possibility that judgment may be postponed.

In the second vision, the disaster is fire, described as consuming the great deep and the land. Here too Amos pleads, “Please stop,” illustrating the recurring pattern of vision, supplication, and mercy.

After the fire vision, the Lord again relents and says, “This too shall not happen.” The repeated cancellation of disaster in the first two visions prepares for the third vision, in which the judgment is not revoked.

In the third vision, the Lord stands beside a wall built with a plumb line, holding a plumb line in his hand—a tool used to test whether a wall is straight. Here, the plumb line symbolizes a precise measurement of the people’s moral condition.
When the Lord asks Amos what he sees, Amos answers, “A plumb line.” Then the Lord says, “I will no longer overlook it”—meaning that Israel’s actions will no longer be ignored.

The judgment will result in the desolation of the high places, the destruction of Israel’s sanctuaries, and the rising up against the house of Jeroboam with the sword. The vision therefore targets both the centers of worship and the royal dynasty.

Amaziah, the priest of Bethel, reports to Jeroboam, king of Israel, that Amos has conspired against him and that his words cannot be tolerated in the land. The report presents Amos’s prophecy as a threat to the religious and royal order.

Amos does not present himself as a professional prophet or a prophet’s son. He describes himself as a herdsman and a dresser of sycamore trees, emphasizing that the Lord took him from his work and commanded him to prophesy to Israel.
